narrative:
The model predicts you have a 61% chance of failing your final year, which is why the school is requiring you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The decision is driven mainly by three key aspects of your situation. By far the strongest factor is that you have already failed one class in the past. Among students who passed, almost none had any previous failures, so this history strongly pushes the prediction toward failing. Two other factors pulled in the opposite direction, slightly lowering the risk: you have a clear desire to pursue higher education, and you report having relatively low amounts of free time after school. Both of these characteristics are more common among students who ultimately pass.

Even though your ambition and limited free time help a little, the impact of your past failure is much larger, which is why the overall prediction leans toward failure.

To improve your chances, focus on breaking the pattern of failing subjects. Use the remedial courses to fill in any gaps from last year, create a realistic weekly study schedule (your current study time is below what most successful students report), and talk to your teachers early about extra support. Small, consistent improvements in how you prepare for classes can quickly change your trajectory.
